title: Phase II Metabolism & Conjugation
summary: How the body tags drugs to flush them out.

lessons.title: Glucuronidation (UGTs)

levels.kid:
When your body wants to remove a drug, it can attach a big sugar-like tag. The tag is called **glucuronic acid**, and attaching it is **glucuronidation**. It is like a label on a package.

The enzymes that attach the tag are called **UGTs**. A tagged drug often mixes with water better, so it can leave in urine or bile. But not every tag switches a drug off. Some tagged forms still work.

Your liver also tags bilirubin, a yellow substance made when old red blood cells are recycled. If one UGT works slowly, bilirubin can build up.

Gut bacteria can remove the tag so a drug can reenter the body. That means a tag is not always the end of the story. Scientists follow where the tagged molecule goes.
levels.hs:
**Glucuronidation** attaches glucuronic acid to a drug or natural substance. The enzymes are **UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs)**, mostly in the endoplasmic reticulum of liver and intestine. Their sugar donor is **UDP-glucuronic acid (UDPGA)**.

A drug can be tagged at an oxygen (O-glucuronide), nitrogen (N-glucuronide) or sulfur (S-glucuronide). This usually increases water solubility and helps excretion into urine or bile, but exceptions exist.

**UGT1A1** conjugates bilirubin; reduced function causes Gilbert syndrome, with mild unconjugated bilirubin elevation. UGT1A1 also glucuronidates SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan. Reduced UGT1A1 function can raise SN-38 exposure and toxicity risk.

**UGT2B7** glucuronidates morphine into morphine-3-glucuronide (mostly not analgesic) and morphine-6-glucuronide (analgesically active). Thus a Phase II product need not be inactive.

Some drug glucuronides enter bile. Gut bacteria can use **β-glucuronidase** to remove the tag; the original drug or metabolite may be reabsorbed, called **enterohepatic recycling**.

Glucuronidation is not automatically "after" oxidation: a molecule with the right group may undergo Phase II directly.
levels.college:
**Chemistry and location.** UGTs are membrane-bound ER enzymes with catalytic domains facing the ER lumen. UDP-glucuronic acid (UDPGA) donates glucuronate, commonly to phenolic/alcohol O, carboxylate O, amino N or thiol S. The reaction creates a β-D-glucuronide via inversion at the anomeric carbon. Transport of UDPGA into the ER lumen and efflux of product can influence overall rate.

**Functional diversity.** Phenolic O-glucuronides are often stable excretion products; carboxylic-acid **acyl glucuronides** can be chemically reactive and are covered in the final lesson. N-glucuronides may be neutral or quaternary cationic depending on N type. UGT1A and UGT2B isoforms differ in substrate preference and tissue distribution.

**Clinical anchors.** UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin and SN-38. The *28 promoter variant reduces expression in some populations; severe loss of UGT1A1 causes Crigler–Najjar syndrome, while milder reductions cause Gilbert syndrome. UGT2B7 contributes to morphine-3- and morphine-6-glucuronide formation; morphine-6-glucuronide retains opioid agonism.

**Enterohepatic cycling.** Biliary glucuronides reaching the intestine can be hydrolyzed by microbial β-glucuronidase, releasing the aglycone for reabsorption. This can prolong exposure or cause local toxicity; SN-38G hydrolysis to SN-38 in the gut contributes to irinotecan-associated diarrhea.

**Developmental nuance.** Neonatal UGT activity is immature, so bilirubin and certain drugs are handled differently from adults. This is not a claim that all UGTs mature at the same time.

**Bottom line.** Conjugation often raises polarity, but product activity, transport and gut deconjugation must be measured.
levels.phd:
**Catalysis.** UGTs are GT-B fold glycosyltransferases using UDPGA, which must reach their ER-luminal catalytic site via transport. Nucleophile activation and SN2-like displacement of UDP yields a β-linked glucuronide from the α-linked UDPGA donor. The enzyme family has overlapping specificity, making a single "responsible UGT" assignment difficult. Allele effects, hepatic disease, transporter function and substrate competition modulate observed clearance.

**Conjugate types.** O-glucuronides of phenols/alcohols increase polarity. Carboxylate O-conjugation makes acyl glucuronides (reactive esters). Tertiary amine N-glucuronidation can produce a permanently charged quaternary product. S-glucuronides form from thiols. Direct C-glucuronidation is rare but possible. Phase II is not equivalent to detoxification.

**UGT1A1 genetics.** Promoter repeat variation (*28, more frequent in some ancestries) reduces expression; coding variant *6 matters in other populations. Partial deficiency leads to Gilbert syndrome; profound deficiency causes Crigler–Najjar. SN-38 competes for UGT1A1 detoxification; reduced activity increases risk of severe irinotecan toxicity. Genetic association does not eliminate the influence of transporters, hepatic function or schedule.

**UGT2B7 and active metabolite.** Morphine-6-glucuronide is a potent μ-opioid agonist with different CNS entry and renal handling from morphine; morphine-3-glucuronide lacks meaningful μ-agonism. Kidney impairment can accumulate both. The analogy "phase II switches off" fails.

**Microbial reversal.** Bacterial β-glucuronidases in gut lumen hydrolyze SN-38G to SN-38; local mucosal exposure contributes to irinotecan GI toxicity. Biliary export (e.g., ABCC2/MRP2) and microbiome enzyme composition shape this pathway.

**Assay design.** Add UDPGA and membrane permeabilization in microsomal UGT assays to address latency; identify conjugate by MS/MS and hydrolysis with β-glucuronidase. Transport and binding can decouple enzyme kinetics from whole-cell disposition.
levels.expert:
**Do not call a conjugate harmless until you test it.** UGT products may be active (morphine-6-glucuronide), unstable (acyl glucuronides) or reactivated by gut bacteria (SN-38G). A metabolite structure and its tissue exposure tell more than a generic "Phase II" label.

**Phenotyping.** For a new candidate with phenolic OH, incubate with human liver and intestinal microsomes plus UDPGA, account for assay latency by permeabilizing membranes, then compare recombinant UGT isoforms. Confirm in hepatocytes and monitor active transport. If a carboxylic acid is conjugated, test acyl-glucuronide migration and protein binding rather than treating it like a stable phenolic O-glucuronide.

**Bilirubin and SN-38.** UGT1A1 links a natural-substrate phenotype (Gilbert syndrome) to drug disposition. Reduced UGT1A1 activity increases unconjugated bilirubin and may raise SN-38 exposure. A patient's jaundice or genotype suggests a pathway but does not quantify individual irinotecan risk without other clinical information.

**Renal/intestinal issues.** Morphine-6-glucuronide remains pharmacologically active, and reduced renal elimination can make it accumulate. Biliary SN-38G delivery plus bacterial β-glucuronidase generates local SN-38, a different tissue-compartment mechanism from high systemic plasma SN-38.

**Development.** Neonates have immature bilirubin conjugation, so adult clearance assumptions cannot simply be reused. UGT isoforms mature differently.

**Interactions.** Enzyme inhibition, induction, substrate competition and transporter inhibition can change the apparent clearance of a glucuronide; separate formation clearance from metabolite elimination. If parent and glucuronide both rise, multiple mechanisms may be operating.

**The decision.** A high glucuronidation fraction may be desirable for predictable clearance only after confirming that the conjugate is stable, excreted, and not active or reactive at clinically relevant exposure.

keyPoints: UGTs attach glucuronic acid from UDPGA in ER lumen
O-, N-, S- and rare C-glucuronides differ; acyl glucuronides can be reactive
UGT1A1 handles bilirubin and irinotecan's SN-38
UGT2B7 forms active morphine-6-glucuronide
Gut β-glucuronidase can deconjugate biliary products, enabling recycling
Phase II may occur directly and does not always inactivate a molecule

examples.tr: Detoxifying conjugation; gut bacteria can regenerate SN-38 locally.
An active Phase II metabolite, countering the 'all conjugates inactive' myth.

lessons.title: Sulfation & acetylation

levels.kid:
The liver has more than one kind of tag. One is a **sulfate** tag, which often helps a molecule mix with water. Another is an **acetyl** tag, a small piece made from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

Different workers attach them. Sulfate workers are called **SULTs**. Acetyl workers are called **NATs**. They need supplies called PAPS and acetyl-CoA, just as an art project needs its materials.

These tags can change how fast a medicine leaves the body or whether it still works. People can inherit faster or slower NAT workers.

A tag does not always make something safer. Sometimes a tagged form can react more easily with cells. That is why scientists check the new tagged molecule, not only the original one.
levels.hs:
**Sulfation** and **acetylation** are Phase II reactions with different enzymes, cofactors and effects.

**Sulfation:** cytosolic sulfotransferases (SULTs) transfer a sulfate group from **PAPS** (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate) to OH or NH groups. The resulting sulfate ester is usually very polar and excreted. Sulfation often has high affinity but limited capacity because PAPS supply can be exhausted; glucuronidation often takes over at higher substrate loads. In infants, sulfation of some compounds matures earlier than glucuronidation.

**Acetylation:** N-acetyltransferases (NAT1/NAT2) transfer an acetyl group from **acetyl-CoA** to arylamines or hydrazines. NAT2 activity varies with inherited genes: slow and rapid acetylators handle some medicines differently. Isoniazid is a NAT2 substrate; slow acetylators can have more exposure. Hydralazine and procainamide are linked to drug-induced lupus, especially in slow acetylators.

Unlike sulfate, an acetyl group often removes a basic NH and can lower water solubility. A reaction called O-acetylation of N-hydroxylated aromatic amines can create reactive intermediates, so acetylation is not always detoxification.

Neither pathway has a simple "always good" or "always bad" rule.
levels.college:
**SULT pathway.** Cytosolic sulfotransferases transfer SO3 from PAPS to phenols, alcohols and some amines; PAP is the coproduct. SULT1A1 handles many phenols, SULT2A1 steroid alcohols, with overlapping specificity. Sulfates are usually highly polar and excreted, but aryl hydroxylamine sulfates can form electrophiles. Sulfation is often high-affinity/low-capacity relative to glucuronidation, with PAPS availability contributing to saturation. Acetaminophen is cleared by both routes; proportions change with age and substrate load without a universal fixed switch.

**NAT pathway.** NAT1/NAT2 are cytosolic enzymes that use acetyl-CoA. A catalytic cysteine is transiently acetylated, then transfers the group to an aromatic amine or hydrazine N. NAT2 polymorphism produces slow, intermediate and rapid acetylator phenotypes, influencing isoniazid and hydralazine disposition. Slow acetylators show higher parent exposure to some drugs and increased risk of certain adverse effects; the precise relationship depends on the drug and pathway. Isoniazid-associated peripheral neuropathy relates to pyridoxine (vitamin B6) depletion; clinical prophylaxis is a medical decision, not a chemical rule.

**Activation risk.** N-hydroxylated arylamines can undergo NAT-mediated O-acetylation, producing labile esters that generate nitrenium ions and DNA adducts. Thus hepatic N-acetylation may detoxify an arylamine, whereas O-acetylation of its N-hydroxy metabolite can bioactivate it in another tissue.

**Physical-property contrast.** Sulfation usually greatly increases ionization; N-acetylation neutralizes an amine and may decrease aqueous solubility. Treat "Phase II = more water-soluble" as a frequent tendency, not a definition.
levels.phd:
**Sulfation kinetics.** PAPS is synthesized from inorganic sulfate and ATP through ATP sulfurylase/APS kinase steps. SULTs act in cytosol; at low concentrations high-affinity SULT routes can dominate some substrates, while UGT routes with higher capacity become more prominent as substrate rises. Substrate inhibition occurs for some SULTs, and PAPS depletion can limit rates. Parent compounds may be sulfated directly; conjugation need not await a CYP oxidation.

**Sulfate bioactivation.** SULT-generated sulfate esters of benzylic alcohols or N-hydroxylated arylamines can be excellent leaving groups, facilitating formation of electrophilic cations or nitrenium ions and DNA adducts. Therefore apparent rapid sulfation does not guarantee benign excretion. Conversely phenolic sulfate conjugates commonly are stable and readily eliminated.

**NAT catalysis.** NAT1/NAT2 use a Cys-His-Asp catalytic triad; acetyl-CoA acetylates Cys, then substrate accepts the acetyl group. NAT2 variation changes protein stability and enzyme function; phenotype is substrate-dependent and influenced by competing pathways. Distinguish arylamine N-acetylation (often detoxifying) from O-acetylation of N-hydroxy arylamines (often bioactivating).

**Isoniazid complexity.** NAT2 acetylates isoniazid to acetylisoniazid; subsequent hydrolysis gives acetylhydrazine, which can undergo further acetylation or oxidation. Hepatotoxicity risk is multifactorial and does not map to "slow is always worse" for every outcome. Pyridoxine depletion contributes to neuropathy.

**Hydralazine/procainamide.** Slow NAT2 acetylation is associated with higher risk of drug-induced lupus for some substrates; immune effects and exposure duration matter.

**Experimental assignment.** Phenotype NAT2 with known probe substrates, verify metabolites by LC-MS and separate SULT vs UGT contributions using selective cofactors and enzyme systems. Do not infer an enzyme solely from the presence of an acetyl or sulfate mass shift.
levels.expert:
**What the team needs to know.** A lead with a phenol may be rapidly sulfated, glucuronidated, or both. Characterize the fractions over a concentration range, not just one assay point: SULT pathways often saturate earlier. Measure PAPS and UDPGA-dependent turnover in appropriate fractions. Intestinal SULT activity and renal excretion can change whole-body predictions.

**Acetylation and pharmacogenetics.** NAT2 genotype influences isoniazid clearance, but exposure, co-medications, nutrition and liver function also matter. Avoid saying a genotype alone determines a clinical outcome. Hydralazine and procainamide associations with lupus are useful signals, not a simple binary prediction.

**A hazard in apparently benign conjugation.** If an arylamine forms an N-hydroxylated metabolite, SULT or NAT O-acetylation can convert the N-OH into a leaving group. Nitrenium ion formation and DNA adducts are possible. Use appropriate genotoxicity assays and metabolite trapping rather than congratulating yourself on fast Phase II clearance. For a stable phenolic sulfate, that concern may be much lower.

**Medicinal chemistry options.** A phenol blocked with F or a methyl can evade sulfation, but changes binding, CYP oxidation and solubility. A basic arylamine susceptible to NAT metabolism could be replaced with an amide or heterocycle, but that may remove a vital target H-bond donor.

**Patient lens.** Sulfation and acetylation can activate, inactivate or redirect molecules. Discuss mechanism and uncertainty rather than giving a universal rule. Relevant lab or genetic information must be interpreted in the context of the actual substrate and all competing pathways.

**Quality gate.** In vitro half-life, stable conjugate ID, reactive-metabolite checks and human-derived systems together justify a pathway claim; none alone is sufficient.

keyPoints: SULTs transfer sulfate from PAPS; sulfates are often highly polar
Sulfation can be high-affinity/low-capacity and may saturate
NAT1/NAT2 transfer acetyl groups from acetyl-CoA
NAT2 polymorphism affects isoniazid and hydralazine handling
N-acetylation may lower solubility; O-acetylation of N-hydroxy arylamines can bioactivate
Phase II reactions need not be detoxifying or strictly sequential

lessons.title: Glutathione conjugation

levels.kid:
Your cells have a helper molecule called **glutathione**, or GSH. Think of it as a catcher wearing a sticky glove. If a drug becomes a reactive piece that might stick to important proteins, GSH can grab it first.

A worker called **GST** helps GSH attach. After that, other workers trim the catcher's long tail, making a smaller piece the body can remove.

This matters for acetaminophen. A little of it turns into a reactive piece called **NAPQI**. Normally GSH catches NAPQI. If GSH is used up, NAPQI can hurt liver cells. Hospitals have a treatment called N-acetylcysteine that helps restore GSH.

GSH is important, but it cannot catch every harmful thing forever. Scientists check how much of a reactive piece forms and whether cells can keep up.
levels.hs:
**Glutathione (GSH)** is a small three-amino-acid molecule: glutamate, cysteine and glycine. The cysteine sulfur is the reactive part. Glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) help GSH attach to electrophiles—electron-hungry molecules that might otherwise react with proteins or DNA.

Targets include epoxides, α,β-unsaturated carbonyls (Michael acceptors) and the acetaminophen metabolite **NAPQI**. GSTs help turn GSH's -SH into a more reactive sulfur nucleophile (thiolate). Some conjugation also occurs without GST.

After conjugation, enzymes remove glutamate and glycine; the remaining cysteine conjugate is acetylated to a **mercapturic acid**, often excreted in urine.

Acetaminophen is mostly cleared by safe conjugation routes, but a small fraction becomes NAPQI through CYPs. GSH normally traps it. When GSH is depleted, NAPQI can bind liver proteins and cause injury. **N-acetylcysteine (NAC)** restores cysteine supply for GSH synthesis and is an established medical antidote.

Do not assume every GSH conjugate is harmless: some can be processed into reactive products, especially in kidney. The specific molecule and pathway matter.
levels.college:
**Chemical basis.** GSH is γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine. Its cysteine thiol attacks electrophiles; GSTs bind GSH and lower the effective thiol pKa to favor the thiolate, positioning it for nucleophilic substitution or Michael addition. Major human GST families include alpha, mu, pi and theta. Spontaneous conjugation can also occur.

**Substrates.** CYP-derived epoxides, α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, quinone imines and alkyl halides are common electrophiles. Acetaminophen's reactive quinone imine NAPQI is normally trapped by GSH. When GSH falls and NAPQI formation outpaces trapping, NAPQI binds hepatic proteins, generating oxidative/mitochondrial stress. N-acetylcysteine supplies cysteine for GSH regeneration and has other protective effects; its clinical use is time-sensitive and supervised.

**Mercapturic acid pathway.** GSH conjugate → γ-glutamyl removal (γ-glutamyltransferase) → glycine removal (dipeptidase) → N-acetylcysteine conjugate (mercapturic acid), usually excreted by kidney.

**Exceptions.** Certain halogenated-alkene GSH conjugates yield cysteine conjugates processed by renal β-lyase to reactive intermediates. A GST pathway can therefore contribute to kidney-specific toxicity.

**Discovery tools.** Incubating drug candidates with human microsomes/hepatocytes plus GSH and detecting GSH adducts by LC-MS flags potential reactive metabolites. A positive trap does not prove clinical toxicity; a negative trap does not exclude all reactive pathways. Complement with protein-adduct studies and exposure data.

**Takeaway.** Phase II conjugation is a chemical route, not a guaranteed safety label.
levels.phd:
**Enzyme and substrate chemistry.** Glutathione's cysteine thiol pKa in solution is relatively high; GST active sites stabilize thiolate and orient electrophilic substrates. The conjugation mechanism may be SN2 at an sp3 carbon, nucleophilic aromatic substitution, or conjugate (Michael) addition, depending on substrate. GSTs are polymorphic and sometimes deleted (e.g., GSTM1-null), but phenotype is not reducible to one allele because enzyme families overlap.

**NAPQI kinetics.** CYP2E1, 1A2 and 3A4 can generate NAPQI from acetaminophen. At low formation rates GSH conjugation competes successfully. With increasing reactive burden, GSH depletion permits NAPQI binding to cysteine residues, especially in mitochondria, triggering oxidative stress, JNK signaling and hepatocellular necrosis. NAC replenishes cysteine for GSH synthesis and can support antioxidant pathways. This explanation is not a dosing guide.

**Mercapturates as biomarkers.** Sequential extracellular processing by γ-glutamyltransferase and dipeptidase yields cysteine conjugates; N-acetyltransferases form N-acetylcysteine conjugates in kidney/liver. Urinary mercapturates indicate that an electrophilic species was intercepted, but do not uniquely quantify protein-adduct burden.

**Bioactivation exception.** GSH conjugation of some halogenated hydrocarbons generates cysteine conjugates that are transported to kidney; cysteine-conjugate β-lyase cleaves them to reactive thiols/thioketenes, causing nephrotoxicity. A protective-looking liver pathway can create a kidney hazard. Some Michael adducts are reversible, allowing parent electrophile regeneration.

**Research assays.** Use GSH and alternate nucleophilic traps, verify structure by MS/MS, investigate time-dependent CYP inhibition and covalent protein labeling. Glutathione adduct intensity depends on trap concentration and ionization efficiency and cannot be read as absolute risk without quantitative calibration. Compare human-derived systems and examine transporter-driven tissue distribution.
levels.expert:
**A warning during lead optimization.** A compound with an electrophilic warhead produces a GSH adduct in microsomes. Decide whether the electrophile is intended to bind a target covalently or is an unwanted reactive metabolite. For intended covalent drugs, balance target-selective reaction kinetics against GSH scavenging and off-target protein adducts. For an unexpected metabolite, identify the CYP soft spot and quantify formation before redesigning.

**Acetaminophen as a systems case.** Most parent follows glucuronidation/sulfation; a minor CYP route produces NAPQI. Healthy GSH usually captures it. When NAPQI generation exceeds detoxification, mitochondrial protein adducts and downstream injury can occur. NAC is a medical antidote that helps restore GSH; this text is mechanistic education, not self-treatment instruction.

**Do not stop at the liver.** A GSH conjugate may travel to kidney, lose its glutamate/glycine groups, then form a reactive β-lyase product. Screen downstream cysteine conjugates if a halogenated motif is present. Conversely, many mercapturic acids are benign excretion products.

**Interpret assay signals carefully.** GSH trapping detects a chemically reactive intermediate under the assay conditions, not necessarily a toxic one in humans. A negative result may miss short-lived, compartment-specific or non-GSH-reactive electrophiles. Confirm with covalent protein labeling, targeted metabolite ID, cross-species comparison and exposure estimates.

**Research priorities.** Reduce unwanted bioactivation without losing target potency; measure unbound liver/kidney exposure and the fraction of reactive pathway relative to safe clearance. A molecule that merely "passes" an in vitro GSH trap may still fail due to transporter-mediated concentration in a sensitive organ.

**Clinical restraint.** If explaining a suspected drug-related liver injury, distinguish chemical plausibility from a patient-specific diagnosis. The metabolite mechanism provides context; clinical assessment requires much more.

keyPoints: GSH is γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine; its cysteine sulfur traps electrophiles
GST enzymes position GSH and favor reactive thiolate
NAPQI from acetaminophen is normally trapped by GSH; depletion risks liver injury
N-acetylcysteine helps replenish GSH and is a medical antidote
Mercapturic acids form after glutamate/glycine removal and N-acetylation
Some GSH conjugates are bioactivated in kidney by β-lyase

lessons.title: Methylation & amino-acid conjugation

levels.kid:
The body has even more ways to tag molecules. One tag is a **methyl** group, a tiny carbon-and-hydrogen piece. A worker takes it from a helper named SAM and puts it on the drug or a natural messenger. This can change how the molecule works.

Another tag is an **amino acid**, one of the small pieces used to build proteins. The body can attach glycine or glutamine to certain acid groups. The new piece may be easier to remove.

For example, the body joins benzoic acid to glycine, making **hippuric acid**. It can leave in urine.

Do not imagine all tags as stickers that simply switch a drug off. A tag can make it work differently, make it leave faster, or even create a problem. Each new product needs checking.
levels.hs:
**Methylation** transfers a -CH3 group from **S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)** to an O, N or S atom; SAM becomes S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH). It often makes a polar OH or NH less able to hydrogen-bond and may reduce water solubility.

**COMT** methylates catechol groups, including levodopa's catechol in peripheral tissues. COMT inhibitors can reduce that peripheral metabolism. **TPMT** methylates thiopurine drugs. People with low TPMT activity can accumulate active thiopurine metabolites and risk bone-marrow suppression; NUDT15 also matters for thiopurine safety.

**Amino-acid conjugation** works differently. First the body activates a carboxylic acid by attaching it to coenzyme A (acyl-CoA). Then an amino acid attacks the acyl group, making an amide. Benzoic acid + glycine → hippuric acid. Phenylacetic acid + glutamine → phenylacetylglutamine, which can carry nitrogen out in urine. Bile acids commonly conjugate with glycine or taurine.

Methylation may decrease polarity; amino-acid conjugation often increases water solubility. They both count as Phase II, showing why Phase II does not mean a single type of chemical change.
levels.college:
**Methyltransferases.** SAM donates a methyl group to O/N/S acceptors and becomes SAH. Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) O-methylates catechols, including peripheral levodopa → 3-O-methyldopa; entacapone reduces peripheral COMT activity. Thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) S-methylates 6-mercaptopurine and related thiopurines; TPMT deficiency can shift metabolism toward cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides and increase myelosuppression. NUDT15 loss of function independently increases thiopurine sensitivity through nucleotide handling. Histamine N-methyltransferase (HNMT) inactivates histamine. Methylation often masks an OH/NH and reduces polarity, but quaternization of a tertiary amine could increase permanent charge.

**Amino acid conjugation.** Carboxylic acids are first activated to acyl-CoA by an ATP-dependent acyl-CoA synthetase. A transferase then forms an amide with glycine, glutamine or taurine. Benzoate → benzoyl-CoA → hippurate (benzoylglycine). Phenylacetate → phenylacetyl-CoA → phenylacetylglutamine; this excretes two nitrogens per glutamine and is used therapeutically in urea-cycle disorders through precursor pathways. Bile acids commonly form glycine/taurine conjugates.

**Salicylate.** Salicylic acid forms salicyluric acid (glycine conjugate), a saturable pathway contributing to nonlinear salicylate elimination alongside other saturable processes.

**Caution.** Acyl-CoA intermediates are reactive and can sometimes acylate proteins. Not every carboxylate undergoes amino-acid conjugation; substrate geometry and enzyme expression decide.

**Big picture.** SAM methylation and amino-acid conjugation are chemically distinct reactions with different effects on polarity and activity. Different conjugation pathways compete for the same starting acid.
levels.phd:
**SAM cycle.** SAM is synthesized from methionine and ATP; methyl donation produces SAH, a product inhibitor for many methyltransferases until hydrolyzed. Methylation can alter hydrogen bonding, electron density, pKa and steric geometry. COMT has membrane-bound and soluble forms and a common Val158Met polymorphism (membrane-bound numbering differs); genotype associations with cognition are context-dependent and not a simple predictor. In levodopa therapy, COMT inhibition reduces peripheral 3-O-methyldopa formation and can extend levodopa exposure.

**TPMT and thiopurines.** TPMT S-methylates 6-mercaptopurine; lower TPMT activity diverts substrate toward thioguanine nucleotide production, increasing myelosuppression risk. Excess methylated metabolites may also be hepatotoxic in high-activity states. NUDT15 sanitizes thioguanine nucleotides; loss of function raises sensitivity even if TPMT is normal. Genotyping and metabolite monitoring answer different questions.

**Acyl-CoA activation.** An acid first forms an acyl-adenylate with ATP, then acyl-CoA with CoA release of AMP and pyrophosphate. Glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT) can transfer acyl groups to glycine; glutamine N-acylation handles phenylacetate. Phenylacetylglutamine urinary loss removes two nitrogen atoms per molecule, an alternate pathway for nitrogen elimination. Taurine conjugation is prominent for bile acids, not a generic fate of all drug acids.

**Saturability.** Salicylate glycine conjugation to salicyluric acid has finite capacity; as concentration rises, clearance can become nonlinear. Distinguish route saturation from the misleading idea that the body simply "stops metabolizing" all salicylate.

**Safety wrinkle.** Acyl-CoA intermediates can react with nucleophilic sites on proteins; changing an acid to avoid acyl glucuronides does not automatically remove acyl-CoA liability. Compare protein adducts and free exposures.

**Method.** Isotope-labeled methyl donors or amino acids, targeted metabolomics and genotyped hepatocyte donors can resolve competing pathways; mass shifts alone do not reveal reaction site.
levels.expert:
**Why a chemist cares about methylation.** If a lead contains a catechol, COMT may rapidly O-methylate it; a catechol can also oxidize to a quinone. Blocking one OH changes both affinity and redox chemistry, so consider whether the two OH groups are essential for target binding. For a thiopurine, TPMT and NUDT15 variation require specialist pharmacogenetic interpretation rather than a blanket claim from genotype alone.

**Clinical examples without dosing.** Entacapone inhibits peripheral COMT and changes levodopa metabolism; tolcapone inhibits central and peripheral COMT but has liver-safety concerns. TPMT deficiency can increase cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotide exposure; NUDT15 variants add independent risk. Phenylacetate-to-phenylacetylglutamine conjugation provides an alternate way to remove nitrogen in urea-cycle disease.

**When an acid disappears but no glucuronide appears.** Look for glycine or glutamine conjugates and their acyl-CoA precursor. A parent carboxylate can enter multiple pathways at once. If salicylate-like elimination becomes concentration-dependent, quantify capacity and competing routes instead of extrapolating a single low-concentration clearance value.

**Assay plan.** Hepatocytes can reveal acyl-CoA and amino-acid conjugation that microsomal UGT-only incubations miss. Track SAM/SAH balance when studying methyltransferases; check enzyme and transporter distribution across target tissues.

**Safety.** Acyl-CoA formation can be part of benign excretion or a source of protein adducts, depending on structure and exposure. An apparent decrease in free parent does not guarantee safety if a reactive intermediate forms.

**Decision.** Choose a scaffold change only after assigning the major conjugation route and asking whether the resulting metabolite is active, reactive or efficiently excreted. This is a multi-pathway assessment, not a single enzyme assay.

keyPoints: SAM supplies methyl groups; SAH is the coproduct
COMT methylates catechols such as peripheral levodopa
TPMT and NUDT15 variation both affect thiopurine safety through different mechanisms
Acid → acyl-CoA → glycine/glutamine/taurine amide conjugate
Benzoate forms hippurate; phenylacetate forms phenylacetylglutamine
Acyl-CoA intermediates may be reactive; salicylate glycine conjugation can saturate

examples.tr: Peripheral O-methylation can be reduced by COMT inhibition.
Glutamine conjugation excretes nitrogen in a urea-cycle bypass.

lessons.title: Acyl glucuronides & reactive conjugates

levels.kid:
Most tags help the body carry molecules away. But one kind of tag can make a drug **reactive** instead.

A drug with an acid piece can get a glucuronic-acid tag. The result is an **acyl glucuronide**. Some acyl glucuronides can move their tag around, like a loose sticker sliding on a box. They may also stick to proteins.

That does not mean every drug with this tag is dangerous. It may be removed quickly. Chemists test whether it sticks to proteins.

Other tags can also surprise us. A sulfate or acetyl tag may sometimes help make a reactive piece; even a glutathione tag can lead to a problem in a different organ. The lesson is simple: follow the product, not just the word "tag."
levels.hs:
A **carboxylic-acid drug** can react with UDP-glucuronic acid via a UGT, giving an **acyl glucuronide**. Unlike many stable phenolic O-glucuronides, an acyl glucuronide is an ester and can be chemically reactive.

It can:

- **Hydrolyze** back to the parent acid.
- **Transacylate** a protein: its acyl group moves to a protein's nucleophilic site, forming a covalent adduct.
- **Migrate** its acyl group to another OH on the glucuronic-acid ring. The resulting isomers can open to aldehyde-containing forms and react with protein amines.

A protein adduct may be harmless or may contribute to toxicity or immune reactions; detection alone does not prove disease. Historically, certain acid-containing anti-inflammatory drugs with reactive acyl glucuronides raised safety concerns.

**Other reactive conjugates:** sulfation or O-acetylation of some N-hydroxylated arylamines can produce short-lived leaving groups and DNA-reactive ions. Some glutathione conjugates become reactive after processing in kidney.

Chemists may replace a carboxylic acid with a tetrazole to avoid acyl glucuronidation, but must check all new metabolites, target potency and exposure. Phase II is not a synonym for safe.
levels.college:
**Acyl glucuronide chemistry.** Carboxylate O attacks UDP-glucuronic acid under UGT catalysis, forming a β-1-O-acyl glucuronide, an ester. It can hydrolyze; its acyl group can undergo intramolecular migration to 2-, 3- or 4-O positions on the sugar. Migration breaks the original glycosidic configuration, allowing ring opening to an aldehyde form.

**Two adduct routes.** Direct transacylation moves the drug acyl group to a protein nucleophile (e.g., Lys). The rearranged glucuronide can form Schiff-base-like adducts through its open-chain aldehyde, followed by stabilization—akin to glycation. Both have been observed in vitro; the relative contribution in vivo varies by drug.

**Risk is not binary.** Reactivity depends on acyl group structure, local pH, protein exposure, rate of clearance and competing hydrolysis. Acyl glucuronides of several carboxylate drugs are formed without obvious idiosyncratic toxicity. Drug-protein adducts can generate immune responses in some contexts, but adduct detection alone does not establish causality. Historically, zomepirac and benoxaprofen are often discussed in this area; their withdrawals cannot be assigned to acyl glucuronides alone without qualification.

**Other conjugation hazards.** SULT or NAT O-acetylation of N-hydroxy arylamines can create electrophilic nitrenium ions; glutathione conjugates of certain halogenated species can yield renal β-lyase toxins.

**Design and assays.** Tetrazole or acyl sulfonamide may remove the carboxylate's acyl-glucuronide route but can shift CYP or N-glucuronidation. Measure conjugate half-life, acyl migration, covalent protein binding and human exposure. Compare matched pairs across potency and safety endpoints.
levels.phd:
**Acyl migration kinetics.** The initial UGT product is a β-1-O-acyl glucuronide. Intramolecular transesterification transfers the acyl group to sugar hydroxyls (2, 3, 4 positions) through neighboring-group chemistry, creating positional and anomeric isomers. Once the anomeric center is freed, the sugar can adopt an open-chain aldehyde, which reacts with lysine ε-amines via imine formation and downstream rearrangements. Direct protein transacylation from the ester is a distinct pathway. Their relative rates depend on aglycone, pH and proteins present.

**Structure-reactivity.** Electron-withdrawing or sterically accessible acyl groups can increase electrophilicity, but reactivity does not map cleanly to one substituent constant. In vitro albumin-adduct formation is a useful hazard signal, not a direct readout of idiosyncratic human toxicity. The hapten hypothesis proposes drug-protein adducts as antigens; immune response also depends on patient genetics, antigen processing and inflammatory context.

**Kinetics vs burden.** A highly reactive conjugate formed in trace amounts and rapidly cleared may produce fewer adducts than a moderately reactive conjugate with high systemic exposure. Distinguish formation clearance (UGT), chemical rearrangement, transporter efflux, albumin binding and renal/biliary excretion. Human hepatocytes and plasma capture different compartments.

**Other reactive Phase II routes.** Sulfate esters of N-hydroxy arylamines can expel sulfate to nitrenium ions. NAT-catalyzed O-acetylation can similarly activate N-hydroxylated substrates. GSH conjugation of some halogenated alkenes gives cysteine conjugates bioactivated by renal β-lyase. These pathways invalidate a universal "conjugation equals detoxification" rule.

**Medicinal-chemistry test.** Acid → tetrazole eliminates acyl glucuronidation but may alter binding, tissue penetration, protein binding and N-glucuronidation. A planned isostere must be judged on free target exposure, new metabolite IDs and safety signals, not just disappearance of the original adduct.
levels.expert:
**What an acyl-glucuronide flag means in a project meeting.** It means a plausible covalent-binding liability, not automatic rejection. Ask: how much conjugate forms in human systems? How fast does it hydrolyze or migrate at physiological pH? What fraction transacylates albumin or other proteins? Is the same adduct seen at relevant exposure? What alternative clearance routes exist?

**Analytical caution.** Acyl migration can continue after blood sampling. Quench and store samples under validated conditions; otherwise an observed mixture of isomers may be a tube artifact rather than in vivo distribution. LC-MS/MS can distinguish some positional isomers with standards; use time-course experiments and NMR when structure is uncertain.

**Clinical causation.** Protein adducts may contribute to immune-mediated injury, but idiosyncratic reactions involve host factors. Zomepirac and benoxaprofen are cautionary case studies, not proof that all acid drugs or acyl glucuronides are unacceptable. Many carboxylate medicines remain valuable.

**What to change.** A tetrazole or acyl sulfonamide can remove the carboxylate acyl-glucuronide route, but recheck potency, pKa, permeability, free fraction and other metabolites. Lowering UGT reactivity by steric shielding may be gentler, yet could increase parent exposure or reroute oxidation. For any proposed fix, compare whole-system exposure and safety rather than one in vitro adduct endpoint.

**Broader principle.** N-hydroxylated arylamines can be activated by SULT/NAT, and some GSH conjugates are kidney-toxic after β-lyase processing. Even familiar "detox" enzymes can produce harmful intermediates. Report what was measured, what remains uncertain, and what experiment would discriminate a real patient risk from a chemical possibility.

keyPoints: Acyl glucuronides are ester conjugates of carboxylic-acid drugs
Acyl migration yields positional isomers and can expose ring-opened aldehyde
Direct transacylation and aldehyde-mediated glycation can form protein adducts
Adduct formation is a hazard signal, not proof of clinical toxicity
Sulfation, acetylation and GSH conjugation can also bioactivate certain substrates
Acid bioisosteres remove one route but may create new liabilities

examples.tr: UGT produces an ester-like conjugate capable of hydrolysis and acyl migration.
Direct transacylation is one protein-binding mechanism.
Phase II groups can become leaving groups that enable DNA-reactive electrophiles.
